questions.stem: An ammeter reads 0.1 A when no current flows through it. This is an example of
questions.explanation: A zero error is a systematic error: every reading taken with this ammeter will be 0.1 A too high, always in the same direction. Repeating the reading cannot remove it — only subtracting 0.1 A from each value can.

distractorRationale.a: Random errors scatter readings above and below the true value; this one shifts them all one way
distractorRationale.c: Parallax comes from viewing the scale at an angle, which is not what is happening when no current flows
distractorRationale.d: The fault is in the instrument, not in how carefully the student reads it

questions.stem: Which of the following best reduces random error in an experiment?

options.text: Taking several readings and finding their mean
Subtracting the zero error from each reading
Recording the answer to more significant figures

questions.explanation: Random errors are equally likely to be positive or negative, so when several readings are averaged the high and low deviations partly cancel and the mean lies closer to the true value. This is the standard reason WAEC practicals ask for repeated readings.

distractorRationale.a: A better instrument improves precision but does not address the scatter caused by the observer
distractorRationale.c: That correction removes a systematic error, not random scatter
distractorRationale.d: Extra digits only make the result look precise; they add no real information

questions.stem: A set of readings that agree closely with one another must be accurate.
questions.explanation: False. Close agreement means the readings are precise, but if the instrument has a zero error or is wrongly calibrated every reading will be wrong by the same amount. Precision describes the spread of readings; accuracy describes their closeness to the true value.

questions.stem: The true length of a rod is 20.0 cm. Four students each take three readings. Whose readings are precise but not accurate?
questions.explanation: Set b has a spread of only 0.1 cm, so it is very precise, but every value is about 1.6 cm below 20.0 cm — a clear systematic shift, so it is inaccurate. This is exactly the pattern produced by an uncorrected zero error.

distractorRationale.a: Tightly grouped and centred on 20.0 cm, so it is both precise and accurate
distractorRationale.c: Widely scattered and centred well away from 20.0 cm, so it is neither precise nor accurate
distractorRationale.d: The mean is exactly 20.0 cm so it is accurate on average, but the 2 cm spread makes it imprecise

questions.stem: A student measures the diameter of a wire as 0.48 mm with a micrometer screw gauge of least count 0.01 mm. Calculate the percentage error in this measurement. Give your answer as a percentage, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Percentage error $= \frac{\Delta d}{d} \times 100 = \frac{0.01}{0.48} \times 100$. Since $\frac{0.01}{0.48} = 0.020833$, the percentage error is $2.08\%$. The uncertainty is taken as the least count of the instrument.

questions.stem: An experiment to find the acceleration of free fall gives 9.4 m/s², while the accepted value is 9.8 m/s². Calculate the percentage error in the experimental result. Give your answer as a percentage, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Percentage error $= \frac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100 = \frac{|9.4 - 9.8|}{9.8} \times 100 = \frac{0.4}{9.8} \times 100$. Since $\frac{0.4}{9.8} = 0.040816$, the percentage error is $4.08\%$. Note the divisor is the accepted value, not the measured one.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are there in the measurement 0.004530 m?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only fix the decimal point and are never significant, so the zeros before the 4 do not count. The significant digits are 4, 5, 3 and the final 0 — the trailing zero after a decimal point is significant because the writer chose to record it. That gives four significant figures.

distractorRationale.a: Counts 4, 5 and 3 but wrongly discards the meaningful trailing zero
distractorRationale.c: Counts the two leading zeros after the decimal point as significant
distractorRationale.d: Counts every digit written, including the zero before the decimal point

questions.stem: A car travels 2.5 m in 4.0 s. Expressed to the correct number of significant figures, its average speed is
questions.explanation: Average speed $= \frac{2.5}{4.0} = 0.625\ \text{m/s}$. Both data values are given to two significant figures, so the answer must also be given to two significant figures: $0.63\ \text{m/s}$.

distractorRationale.a: Rounded to one significant figure, throwing away information the data supports
distractorRationale.c: The raw calculator value, which claims three significant figures the data cannot justify
distractorRationale.d: Adds a further meaningless zero, claiming four significant figures

questions.stem: A rectangular card is measured as 4.0 cm ± 0.1 cm long and 2.0 cm ± 0.1 cm wide. Calculate the percentage error in the calculated area of the card. Give your answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: For a product, percentage errors add. Percentage error in length $= \frac{0.1}{4.0} \times 100 = 2.5\%$; percentage error in width $= \frac{0.1}{2.0} \times 100 = 5.0\%$. Total percentage error in the area $= 2.5 + 5.0 = 7.5\%$. The shorter side dominates, so improving the width measurement would help most.

questions.stem: In a pendulum experiment the length is measured as 100.0 cm ± 0.1 cm and the period as 2.0 s ± 0.1 s. Which statement about the errors is correct?

options.text: The length contributes the larger percentage error, because 0.1 cm is a larger uncertainty than 0.1 s
Both contribute equally, because both uncertainties are 0.1
The period contributes the larger percentage error, so the timing should be improved first
Neither contributes any error, because both were measured with laboratory instruments

questions.explanation: Percentage error in length is $\frac{0.1}{100.0} \times 100 = 0.1\%$, while percentage error in the period is $\frac{0.1}{2.0} \times 100 = 5.0\%$. The period is fifty times worse, so timing more oscillations is the single most useful improvement.

distractorRationale.a: Compares raw uncertainties instead of relative ones; the units are different so a direct comparison is meaningless
distractorRationale.b: Percentage error depends on the size of the quantity measured, not just the uncertainty
distractorRationale.d: Every instrument has a finite precision, so uncertainty is always present

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes systematic errors?

options.text: They occur due to random fluctuations in measurement.
They arise from imperfections in the measurement system.
They can be reduced by repeating measurements.
They are always equal in magnitude.

questions.explanation: Systematic errors are consistent and repeatable inaccuracies that occur due to flaws in the measurement system or methodology. Unlike random errors, they do not vary from one measurement to another and can often be identified and corrected.

distractorRationale.a: This describes random errors, not systematic errors.
distractorRationale.c: Repeating measurements can help reduce random errors, not systematic errors.
distractorRationale.d: Systematic errors do not have to be equal in magnitude.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines precision in measurements?

questions.explanation: Precision refers to the consistency of repeated measurements. If repeated measurements yield similar results, the measurements are considered precise, regardless of how close they are to the true value.

distractorRationale.a: This definition describes accuracy, not precision.

distractorRationale.d: The difference between the highest and lowest measurements relates to range, not precision.

questions.stem: A thermometer reads 25.0 °C in a room where the actual temperature is 26.5 °C. Calculate the percentage error.
questions.explanation: Percentage error is calculated using the formula: |(Measured Value - True Value) / True Value| × 100%. Here, it is |(25.0 - 26.5) / 26.5| × 100% = 5.66%, which rounds to 6.0%.

distractorRationale.a: This is a close approximation but not correctly calculated.
distractorRationale.c: This option overestimates the percentage error.
distractorRationale.d: This option significantly overestimates the percentage error.
